inline.s: [No Essential Nature] All dharmas are illusory; no essential nature can be spoken of. "Essential nature" means a substantial entity.

This teaching of the World-Honored One sets aside the provisional and returns to the real: it is beyond all words and speech, where practice arises and understanding is cut off, and one enters directly into the unborn.

[Sariputra, why does the Tathagata speak of the foundations of mindfulness? Sariputra, the sutra says that if a person who has attained the four foundations of mindfulness could thereby attain the essential nature of all dharmas, could attain his own self, could attain a self, could attain a person — this is impossible. It is in order to reveal the distinguishing characteristics of dharmas as empty that he speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness. The nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is without nature, without location, without thought, without speech, without greed or attachment. If the very nature of mindfulness is not to be had, how much less the foundations of mindfulness! Therefore the Tathagata calls them the foundations of mindfulness.]

Sariputra, since all speech is called wrong, why then does the Tathagata say that there are foundations of mindfulness? Sariputra, although the Tathagata speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness, he never says that if a person attains the four foundations of mindfulness, that person can attain the essential nature of all dharmas, can attain his own self, can attain a self, can attain a person. It is in order to reveal the distinguishing characteristics of dharmas that the Tathagata speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness. The very nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is without nature, without location, without thought, without speech, without greed or attachment. If the nature of mindfulness itself is not to be had, how much less can there be foundations of mindfulness! This is what the Tathagata means by the foundations of mindfulness (what the Tathagata speaks of is the foundations of mindfulness as a mere designation, not foundations of mindfulness that truly exist).

[The foundations of mindfulness] Mindfulness is the observing wisdom; the foundation is the object observed. To observe the object with wisdom is called the foundation of mindfulness. [The four foundations of mindfulness] The foundation of mindfulness of body, of feeling, of mind, and of dharmas. The foundation of mindfulness of body is the contemplation that the body is impure; of feeling, the contemplation that feeling is suffering; of mind, the contemplation that mind is impermanent; of dharmas, the contemplation that dharmas are without self. [The distinguishing characteristics of all dharmas] "Distinguishing characteristics" means the characteristics by which things differ from one another. "The distinguishing characteristics of all dharmas" means the characteristics by which dharmas differ from one another. All dharmas are illusions, like things in a dream. The mark of an illusion is this: the characteristic appears, but the essence is absent. Though their distinguishing characteristics are manifold and each one different, their shared characteristic is a single characteristic: ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.

[Sariputra, if dharmas had a definite essential nature — even one so subtle as a hundredth part of a split hair — then the Buddhas would not appear in the world, nor would they ever teach that the nature of all dharmas is empty.]

Sariputra, if dharmas had any substantial entity, even one as subtle as a hundredth part of a single hair, the Buddhas would not appear in the world, nor would they ever say that the nature of all dharmas is empty.

The meaning is this: precisely because dharmas have no substantial entity do the Buddhas appear in the world and teach that all dharmas are without substance, are illusions, are things in a dream (the emptiness of the nature of all dharmas). Living beings all dwell within the dream of ignorance; because they have never once awakened, they do not know that they are dreaming at all, but take the things in the dream (all dharmas) to be real. Seduced by them and oppressed by them, they act accordingly and so create karma, and thus suffer without end and revolve in birth and death unceasingly. The Buddhas are the Greatly Awakened Ones; therefore they appear in the world to tell living beings the true characteristics of all dharmas and to ferry them out of the dream and beyond suffering.

[Sariputra, all dharmas are truly empty, without nature, of one characteristic — namely, no characteristic. The Tathagata sees this fully, and therefore says that there are foundations of mindfulness.]

Sariputra, all dharmas are truly empty (originally there is not a single thing), they have no essential nature, and in their essential nature they are a single characteristic: the so-called no-characteristic. The Tathagata sees this fully, and therefore says that there are foundations of mindfulness.
In terms of characteristics, all dharmas are a vast multitude of appearances; in terms of essence, they are a single characteristic — no characteristic.

[Sariputra, the foundations of mindfulness are called no place and no non-place, without thought and without the karma of thought, without perception and without discrimination, without intention and without the karma of intention, without mentation and without the karma of mentation, without dharma and without the characteristics of dharmas; all of them are neither gathered nor dispersed. Therefore the sages and noble ones, being without discrimination, are said to have the foundations of mindfulness. It is for this reason that the Tathagata says that there are foundations of mindfulness: in accord with nothing whatsoever, it is called the foundations of mindfulness; in accord with Buddha-recitation, it is called the foundations of mindfulness.]

Sariputra, the foundations of mindfulness are in truth no place and no non-place, without thought and without the karma of thought, without perception and without discrimination, without intention and without the karma of intention, without mentation and without the karma of mentation, without dharma and without the characteristics of dharmas; all of them are neither gathered nor dispersed. Therefore the sages and noble ones, by being without discrimination, are said to have the foundations of mindfulness. It is on this account that the Tathagata says that there are foundations of mindfulness: in accord with nothing whatsoever, it is called the foundations of mindfulness; in accord with nothing whatsoever, to recite the Buddha's name is called the foundations of mindfulness.

[Karma] That which is done by body, speech, and mind. [Sages and noble ones] The bodhisattva's cultivation passes through fifty-two stages: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of abiding, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, the stage of equal enlightenment, and the stage of wondrous enlightenment, wondrous enlightenment being Buddhahood. Among these, the ten stages of abiding, the ten stages of practice, and the ten stages of dedication are the sages (the three stages of the sages); the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment are the noble ones.

Therefore the sages and noble ones, being without discrimination, are said to have the foundations of mindfulness." These words are of the utmost importance! This is the gateway to actual practice. "The Buddha said: Mahamati, the bodhisattva mahasattva, relying on the noble teachings, is without discrimination. Dwelling alone in quiet seclusion, he contemplates his own awareness, awakened not through another; free from views of discrimination, he rises higher and higher and enters the Tathagata's realm. Such cultivation is called the aspect of the practice of self-realized noble wisdom." (Lankavatara Sutra)

Ordinarily, observing an object with wisdom is called the foundation of mindfulness. Yet from the standpoint of the true characteristics of all dharmas, all dharmas are illusory; there is neither wisdom nor object. Therefore the sages and noble ones, being without discrimination, are said to have the foundations of mindfulness; and in accord with nothing whatsoever, Buddha-recitation is called the foundations of mindfulness.

[Sariputra, what is called Buddha-recitation? To see nothing whatsoever is called Buddha-recitation. Sariputra, the Buddhas are immeasurable, inconceivable, beyond all reckoning; for this reason, to see nothing whatsoever is called Buddha-recitation. In truth, the name is without discrimination, and the Buddhas are without discrimination; therefore it is said: to be mindful without discrimination is itself Buddha-recitation.]

Sariputra, what is meant by Buddha-recitation? To see nothing whatsoever is called Buddha-recitation. Sariputra, the Buddhas are immeasurable, inconceivable, and beyond all reckoning; for this reason, to see nothing whatsoever is called Buddha-recitation. In truth, the Buddha's name is without discrimination and the Buddhas are without discrimination; therefore it is said that to be mindful without discrimination is itself Buddha-recitation.

[To see nothing whatsoever is called Buddha-recitation] This is Buddha-recitation of true characteristics. There are four methods of Buddha-recitation: 1. Holding the name, single-mindedly calling the Buddha's name; 2. Contemplating the image, facing an image of the Buddha and calling to mind the Buddha's marks and excellences, his light, and so forth; 3. Contemplation, visualizing according to the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; 4. Buddha-recitation of true characteristics, as the passage below says: "What is called the true characteristics of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever. One recites the Buddha's name by means of this ultimately empty, nothing-whatsoever Dharma." For further discussion of Buddha-recitation of true characteristics, see the appendix at the end of this book: "A Teaching to the Assembly at the Intensive Seven-Day Retreat" by Master Xingce, the Tenth Patriarch of the Pure Land school.

Buddha-recitation may also be divided into: exclusive mindfulness of the self-Buddha (the Buddha of one's own nature), exclusive mindfulness of the other-Buddha (Amitabha Buddha of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss), and the combined mindfulness of the self-Buddha and the other-Buddha. On this, Master Yinguang says:
The one practice of Buddha-recitation is the all-embracing dharma-gate of Buddhism.
It differs only in that there is exclusive mindfulness of the self-Buddha, exclusive mindfulness of the other-Buddha, and combined mindfulness of both.

Exclusive mindfulness of the self-Buddha: as in the various sutras, one penetrates deeply into true characteristics in the hope of realizing and awakening to them. Within the five aggregates, the six sense-entrances, the twelve sense-fields, the eighteen elements, the seven great elements, and all such dharmas, one illumines with the wisdom of prajna and thoroughly understands that all these dharmas are, in their very substance, entirely empty, and so one personally sees the wondrous true-suchness nature that is inherently present. This also includes the Chan practice of investigating "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" and the various huatou, in the hope of personally seeing one's original face before one's parents were born. Among the four kinds of Buddha-recitation, this is called Buddha-recitation of true characteristics.

Exclusive mindfulness of the other-Buddha has three methods of mindfulness. First, visualization: according to the sixteen-contemplation sutra (that is, the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life) one performs the contemplation, either contemplating solely the white curl of light between the brows, or contemplating only a Buddha-body of one zhang and six chi or of eight chi, or contemplating the vast dharmakaya, or performing all sixteen contemplations. Second, contemplating the image: facing an image of the Buddha, one calls to mind the Buddha's marks and excellences, his light, and so forth. Third, holding the name: single-mindedly one calls the holy name of Amitabha Buddha. Though these three kinds of Buddha-recitation differ in method, all require true faith and urgent vows before one can resonate with the Buddha and be in communion with him, and only then can one be certain to leave this Saha World in this present life and be born in that Land of Ultimate Bliss. Among these four kinds of Buddha-recitation, only Buddha-recitation of true characteristics has the profoundest principle, yet it is by no means easy to cultivate, since one relies solely on one's own precepts, concentration, and wisdom and on the power of investigation and illumination, with no other power to assist. If one's roots from former lives are not mature, then even to awaken is not easy, how much less to realize it in truth. Only holding the name in Buddha-recitation is the easiest to begin and the swiftest to succeed. If one can gather in all six sense-faculties and let pure mindfulness continue unbroken, one will certainly realize the samadhi of Buddha-recitation in this very life, and at the end of life be certainly reborn in the highest grade. Even if one's capacities are dull and one has not realized samadhi, then simply by holding the Buddha's name with faith and vows — as a child recalls its mother, constantly and without interval — when the end of life comes, one resonates with the Buddha and, relying on the Buddha's compassionate power, is reborn with one's karma carried along. For beings in the Dharma-ending age, this alone is what they can rely on. Otherwise one merely plants a cause for the future and finds it hard to gain true benefit. If one can truly recite with all one's heart, and recite until the whole mind is Buddha and the whole Buddha is mind, until outside the mind there is no Buddha and outside the Buddha there is no mind, until one is mindful yet not mindful, not mindful yet mindful, when mind and Buddha are both revealed and yet both dissolved — then the wondrous principle of true characteristics is directly revealed, and the dependent and principal rewards of the Western Pure Land are perfectly made manifest. Thus, while holding the name one penetrates deeply into true characteristics, and without performing contemplation one personally sees the West. It embraces the widest range of capacities, yields the deepest benefit, suits best the dull-rooted people of the Dharma-ending age, and greatly fulfills the Tathagata's purpose in appearing in the world. For this reason, the masters of old for the most part placed their emphasis on the single gate of holding the name. Such is the general outline of mindfulness of the other-Buddha.

As for mindfulness of both self and other, this is what is called the dual cultivation of Chan and Pure Land. There are those who simply investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" in the hope of clarifying the mind and seeing the nature, and who do not make it their business to seek rebirth through faith and vows; though this resembles the dual cultivation of Chan and Pure Land, it is in fact Chan without Pure Land. Lacking faith and vows, they have no way to rely on the Buddha's power to be reborn with their karma carried along. And if they have not reached the stage where karma is exhausted and feelings are emptied, they cannot rely on their own power to end birth and death either. Thus we know that in the dual cultivation of Chan and Pure Land, only those with profound faith and vows can benefit; otherwise one is certainly better off devoting oneself exclusively to the single gate of holding the Buddha's name." (Preface to the Sacred Canon of Amitabha)

[The seven great elements] Earth, water, fire, wind, space, seeing, and consciousness. Earth, water, fire, and wind are the four great elements; space is the nature of empty space; seeing is the seeing nature of the eye-faculty (by extrapolation from this one, the hearing nature of the ear-faculty and the rest can be understood; the great element of seeing is the nature of the six faculties); consciousness is the eight consciousnesses. Because these seven pervade the dharma-realm, they are called great.

[Furthermore, to see the true characteristics of all dharmas is called seeing the Buddha. What is called the true characteristics of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever. One recites the Buddha's name by means of this ultimately empty, nothing-whatsoever Dharma.]

Furthermore, to see the true characteristics of all dharmas is called seeing the Buddha. What are the true characteristics of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever. It is by means of this ultimately empty, nothing-whatsoever Dharma that one recites the Buddha's name.

[Furthermore, within such a Dharma, even a subtle thought is not to be had; this is called Buddha-recitation. Sariputra, this Dharma of Buddha-recitation cuts off the path of speech, goes beyond all thoughts, and is not to be grasped by thought; this is called Buddha-recitation.]

Furthermore, within this Dharma of "reciting the Buddha's name by means of the ultimately empty, nothing-whatsoever Dharma," not even a subtle thought is to be had; this is called Buddha-recitation. Sariputra, this Dharma of Buddha-recitation cuts off the path of speech, goes beyond all thoughts, and is not to be grasped by thought; this is called Buddha-recitation.

[Sariputra, all thoughts whatsoever have the characteristic of still extinction. To accord with this Dharma — this is called cultivating Buddha-recitation. One cannot recite the Buddha by means of form. Why? To be mindful of form is to grasp at characteristics; to savor its flavor is consciousness. To be without shape and without form, without object and without nature — this is called Buddha-recitation. Therefore you should know: to be without discrimination, without grasping and without rejecting, is true Buddha-recitation.]

Sariputra, all thoughts whatsoever have the characteristic of still extinction. To accord with this Dharma is called cultivating Buddha-recitation. One cannot recite the Buddha by means of form. Why? To be mindful of form is to grasp at characteristics; to savor its flavor is consciousness. To be without shape and without form, without object and without nature — this is called Buddha-recitation. Therefore you should know that to be without discrimination, without grasping and without rejecting, is true Buddha-recitation.

inline.s: [Then Sariputra said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, how is it that one who also teaches this Dharma to others is an evil spiritual friend? World-Honored One, how is it that one who also teaches this Dharma to others is a good spiritual friend?]

Then Sariputra reverently asked the Buddha: World-Honored One, how is it that one who teaches this Dharma of true characteristics to others is an evil spiritual friend? World-Honored One, how is it that one who
also
teaches this Dharma of true characteristics to others is a good spiritual friend?

[The Buddha told Sariputra: If a bhikshu teaches another bhikshu: 'Bhikshu, you should now know that Buddha-recitation is the emptying of thought; the object on which it focuses should not be thought upon. Even the thought that empties thought is itself empty; this is the emptiness of no-nature, which can cut off the perception of form and can cut off the perception of grasping.' At that time such a person has no attainment and no perception, how much less any dwelling upon thought! At that time such a person is entirely without anything whatsoever, still and extinct, without nature, gathering no perceptions, extinguishing all dharmas — this is called cultivating Buddha-recitation.]

The Buddha said to Sariputra: If a bhikshu teaches another bhikshu: 'Bhikshu, you should know that Buddha-recitation is the emptying of thought, and that the object on which it focuses should not be clung to in thought. Moreover,
the thought that empties thought'
— that thought

is emptied as well; this is absolute emptiness (the emptiness of no-nature), which can cut off the perception of form and can cut off the perception of grasping.' At that time such a person has nothing to attain and nothing to perceive, how much less any dwelling of thought! At that time such a person is entirely without anything whatsoever, still and extinct, without nature, gathering no perceptions, extinguishing all dharmas (when perception is extinguished, all dharmas are extinguished) — this is called cultivating Buddha-recitation.

[Buddha-recitation is called the breaking of all evaluation and observation, whether wholesome or unwholesome; to be without evaluation and without observation, still and without perception, is called Buddha-recitation. Why? One should not recollect the Buddhas by means of evaluation and observation; to be without evaluation and without observation is called pure Buddha-recitation. Within this mindfulness there is not even the subtlest karma of mind and mental engagement, how much less the karma of body and speech!]

[Evaluation and observation] The new translations render this as vitarka and vicara; the old translations render it as evaluation and observation. Coarse thought is called evaluation, subtle thought is called observation; both can disturb the concentrated mind.

[Again, one who recites the Buddha's name is free from all perceptions, and perceptions do not abide in the mind. Without discrimination, without names, without obstruction, without desire and without attainment, one does not give rise to evaluation and observation. Why? Sariputra, whatever perceptions arise in dependence on what is thought
are all wrong views. Sariputra, in accord with nothing whatsoever, without evaluation and without observation, without arising and without ceasing
One who penetrates this is called Buddha-recitation. In such mindfulness there is no greed, no attachment, no opposition, no compliance, no name and no perception.

mind. Without discrimination, without names, without obstruction, without desire and without attainment, one does not give rise to evaluation and observation. Why? Sariputra, whatever perceptions arise in dependence on what is thought

Buddha-recitation
there is no greed, no attachment, no opposition, no compliance, no name and no perception.
[One who penetrates this is called Buddha-recitation] One who penetrates such a Dharma of true characteristics is called Buddha-recitation — that is, Buddha-recitation of true characteristics.

Sariputra, to be without perception and without speech is what is called Buddha-recitation. Within it there is not even a subtle and tiny thought, how much less the coarse karma of body, speech, and mind! Where there is no karma of body, speech, and mind, there is no grasping and no rejecting, no contention and no dispute, no thought and no discrimination; empty, still, and without nature, with all evaluation and observation extinguished — this is called Buddha-recitation.]
Sariputra, to be without perception and without speech is what is called Buddha-recitation. Within it there is not

karma of body, speech, and mind! Where there is no karma of body, speech, and mind, there is no grasping and no rejecting, no contention and no dispute, no thought and no discrimination; empty, still, and without nature, with all evaluation and observation extinguished — this is called Buddha-recitation.

[Sariputra, if a person accomplishes such mindfulness, and wishes to transform the land of the four continents, he can transform it at will, and can also subdue a hundred thousand million maras — how much more so the wretched ignorance that arises from false and deceptive conditions and has no fixed characteristic! This Dharma is thus
without perception and without idle discourse, without arising and without ceasing, inexpressible, beyond discrimination, without darkness and without light

[The four continents] The four great continents to the east, south, west, and north of Mount Sumeru (the eastern continent of Purvavideha, the southern continent of Jambudvipa, the western continent of Aparagodaniya, and the northern continent of Uttarakuru). [Wretched and evil] Vile. [One characteristic] The single true characteristic.

[Why? The Tathagata is not called form, not called perception, not called thought, not called discrimination, neither opposed nor compliant, neither grasping nor rejecting, neither concentration nor wisdom, neither illumination nor non-illumination. The Tathagata is inexpressible, inconceivable, without characteristic. You should now take no delight in grasping at characteristics, take no delight in idle discourse. The Buddha, in regard to all dharmas, is without attachment and without measure, and does not see any dharma that can be attached to or measured. Such a person cannot even attain the Buddha, how much less thought!]
Why?
Because

the Tathagata is not called form, not called perception, not called thought, not called discrimination, neither opposed nor compliant, neither grasping nor rejecting, neither concentration nor wisdom, neither illumination nor non-illumination. The Tathagata is inexpressible, inconceivable, without characteristic. You should now

Sariputra, one who teaches thus is called a good spiritual friend. In the supreme meaning there is no fixed thing that is a good spiritual friend or an evil spiritual friend.]

originally there is not a single thing; how could there be good or evil? Therefore there is no such thing as a good spiritual friend or an evil spiritual friend.

[Furthermore, Sariputra, if a bhikshu teaches another bhikshu: 'Bhikshu, you should discriminate and observe all dharmas, yet do not think upon the characteristics of dharmas.' If a bhikshu cultivates thus, with a mind free of attachment, he can penetrate the one characteristic of all dharmas, the so-called no-characteristic. Such a person does not even give rise to the perception of dharmas, how much less the perception of self and of persons!]

[Sariputra, what do you think? One who thinks upon the perception of dharmas — can such a person extinguish all dharmas? No, World-Honored One.
Shariputra, what do you think? One who thinks upon the perception of dharmas — can such a person extinguish all dharmas? Shariputra replied: No, World-Honored One.

This passage means: those who think upon the perception of dharmas, because they dwell in and attach to dharmas, cannot extinguish all dharmas. The next passage speaks of another case: those who do not give rise to the perception of attaining dharmas and do not give rise to the perception of thinking upon dharmas — because they have already penetrated that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever, and unattainable, there is no dharma to extinguish, and so they too cannot extinguish all dharmas, just as a tree without roots cannot have branches, leaves, flowers, or fruit.
Shariputra, if a tree has no root

can it have branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit? No, World-Honored One. Even so, Shariputra, if a person does not attain the root of all dharmas, can that person give rise to the perception of dharmas? No, World-Honored One. Sariputra, if a person does not attain the non-thinking of the perception of dharmas, can that person extinguish all dharmas? No, World-Honored One. Such a person does not attain dharmas, does not attain the characteristics of dharmas, does not attain extinction, and does not discriminate; without arising and without ceasing
At that time such a person neither arises nor ceases, is not called one who attains nirvana, nor is he called one who does not attain nirvana.
The Buddha asked: Sariputra, if a tree has no root,
can it have flowers

The Buddha asked: Even so, Sariputra, if a person does not attain the root of all dharmas, can that person give rise to the perception of dharmas? Sariputra replied: No, World-Honored One.

The Buddha asked: Sariputra, if a person does not give rise to the perception of attaining dharmas and does not give rise to the perception of thinking upon dharmas, can that person extinguish all dharmas? [Furthermore, Sariputra, right view is called right action, right practice, the right way, and right understanding; it is without distortion, seeing things as they truly are. Therefore the Tathagata speaks of it as right view. Sariputra, if living beings are without distortion and contemplate things as they truly are, they have right view. If they give rise to the perception of a self, the perception of a person, or the perception of a being, you should know that such people are all practicing wrongly.

Shariputra, the Buddha and the Buddha's disciples do not speak of a self, do not speak of a person, do not speak of a being, do not speak of a lifespan, do not speak of the view of annihilation or the view of permanence;
therefore
the Buddha and the Buddha's disciples are called right view. Why? Because their right contemplation
is
undistorted.
[The two views of annihilation and permanence] The "view of annihilation" holds that the self is limited to a single lifetime and falls into utter extinction at death (
that there is nothing left at all
); the "view of permanence" holds that after death the self is not extinguished but can be reborn and continue in its present state.

[Sariputra, among all ordinary beings, none can enter into this matter. Why? All ordinary beings are entirely without right view. They have only the compliant patience that accords with right view, and cannot see things as they truly are. Sariputra, this is called the difference between right view and wrong view. Because one sees things as they truly are, it is called right view. To see the causes of worldly happiness and to seek the growth of wealth and profit is worldly right view; all of it is deceptive and does not escape birth and death. Sariputra, what the Buddha calls worldly right view is a teaching for the indolent and inferior.]
